findings.detail: D4 [verdict (pilot conditions); alternatives 'Staged or limited rollout'; practicalImplications[3]] The decision objective explicitly asks for conditions with 'named compensating controls, contractual or evidence deliverables, deadlines'. The draft names the controls and deliverables but gives no deadlines for any vendor deliverable apart from 'before Friday' for the written request. It also sets no pilot parameters: no population size or cap, no duration, no exit or expansion criteria, and no trigger for rolling back if deliverables slip. The draft itself flags the risk that a 'pilot quietly becomes permanent', but it never defines the guardrail that would prevent it.

D7 [CL9; practicalImplications[4]; edgeCasesAndFailureModes[8]] Data residency and the privacy/DPA side of placing the employee directory with this vendor are listed in criterion G6 but left out of CL9 and the legal action item. Availability SLA and outage resilience for a tier-0 dependency appear only as a one-line edge case. Neither becomes a condition.

D5 [CL6; C2 mechanisms] CL6 calls BW-11 'not a defensible accepted risk'. That is stated more firmly than the evidence allows. The basis is a snippet of the superseded 800-63-3 text (E11), which is federal guidance rather than a binding standard for a private workforce IdP. The executive summary also gives no detail on why the tester accepted the risk; compensating controls such as lockout elsewhere or a different OTP length are possible. The conclusion is probably right but should be hedged. The K4 illustration also assumes a 6-digit OTP, which is not in the evidence. The draft does label this as an assumption.

D1 [verdict (sentence 4); CL2; C1 assessment] The verdict says 'none of the tier-0 surfaces going to production has been independently tested'. The sources do not support that. The web SAML/OIDC login flows and the admin console were in scope of the Brightwater test (E1), and both are tier-0 surfaces. That test is old and may not reflect the current code, but the honest statement is that the tested surfaces are 32 months stale and may have changed (the changelog is only an excerpt), while SCIM, the session service, the device grant and passkeys were never tested. The same overreach shows up in CL2 ('the code going to production on these surfaces') and in the C1 line 'Every major surface changed since then was untested'. These read as if the changelog were complete and the login and admin code were known to be unchanged or known to be changed. Neither is established.

D8 [CL14; K3] CL14 and K3 ('C1 to C4 carry 75% of the decision weight') do no work. The draft never scores the criteria and never says how the weights change the decision, so the figure adds an appearance of rigour without effect. Either score the options against the weighted criteria or drop it.

D2 [counterarguments; tradeoffs[0], tradeoffs[1]; alternatives] The strongest case for approval is never addressed: the risk of the status quo. The draft does not ask what the organisation uses today for 2,300 employees (no SSO, a legacy IdP, manual provisioning or slow deprovisioning). It does not weigh whether delay keeps a weaker posture in place, such as password sprawl or orphaned accounts after terminations. 'Deferral protects all 2,300 accounts' (tradeoffs) assumes the current state is safer, without evidence. The staging tradeoff also assumes there is an existing IdP ('two IdP paths') without checking.

D3 [alternatives; practicalImplications] Obvious decision options are missing. (a) Approve SSO separately from SCIM, for example SSO only, with JIT or existing-tool provisioning until provisioner-v2 is tested. This follows directly from the draft's own finding that SCIM is the least-assured surface; at present it only appears as a parenthetical ('SCIM limited to a non-critical app'). (b) A customer-commissioned independent test of its own Keystone tenant (SCIM, device grant, session invalidation, OTP rate limiting) during a pilot. This would not depend on the vendor's cooperation, which the draft treats as the main bottleneck. (c) Evaluating alternative IdP vendors if Keystone cannot provide assurance.

D6 [criteriaAssessments C1 strengths[0]] The C1 strength 'A credible-sounding third-party firm' has no supporting evidence. Nothing in the packet speaks to Brightwater's credibility or accreditation, and E1 only names the firm. This sits awkwardly next to the draft's own authenticity concern (CL13).

openDecisiveGaps: What IdP and provisioning arrangement does the organisation use today, and what is its security posture (MFA coverage, deprovisioning latency)? This sets the relative risk of deferral versus a staged rollout.
Can Keystone ID disable the Device Authorization Grant per tenant, enforce passkey-only or phishing-resistant MFA, restrict admin export, scope SCIM tokens and stream audit events to a SIEM?

Does a retest letter or other independent evidence exist that BW-04, BW-07 and BW-11 are closed on the current session service, and does Keystone hold a SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 attestation whose scope covers provisioner-v2?
Will the vendor permit a customer-commissioned penetration test of the customer's own tenant, including SCIM provisioner-v2, before or during a pilot?
Is the full signed Brightwater report, obtained directly from Brightwater, consistent with the vendor-supplied summary (scope, finding IDs, severities, statuses)?
